strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated, analysis-driven contribution: the empirical studies of the input/weight loss landscape (Figure 2), layer-wise feature interpolation (Figure 3, Figure 7 in appendix), and frequency-band masking over the course of optimisation (Figure 4) are interesting and go beyond a pure 'method paper', giving a plausible mechanistic account of why optimisation-based visual jailbreaks transfer poorly.

The proposed FORCE method (layer-aware regularisation + spectral rescaling) follows directly from the analysis, and each component is ablated independently (Table 3), showing the spectral component contributes more than the layer component.

The evaluation is broad in target coverage: three adapter-based MLLMs, two early-fusion MLLMs, and three commercial models (Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5), across three benchmarks (MaliciousInstruct, AdvBench, HADES), with both semantic and blank initialisation and a strict zero-shot setting.

Evaluation methodology is more careful than much of this literature: substring matching combined with an LLM judge (HarmBench classifier) to avoid false positives, and query cost is reported alongside ASR.

The paper includes appropriate responsible-disclosure elements (harm warning, ethics statement, LLM usage disclosure) and a reasonable reproducibility statement with hyperparameters and algorithms in the appendix.
weaknesses: The analysis and the method are developed and validated on a single source model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B). It is unclear whether the layer-reliance and spectral-reliance phenomena, and hence the effectiveness of FORCE, generalise to other source architectures; this materially limits the claimed generality of the findings.

Improvements on the most practically important targets (commercial MLLMs) are extremely small in absolute terms (e.g., ASR 1.00→2.00 on GPT-5, 1.00→2.00 on Claude-Sonnet-4), yet are reported as '100%' or '200%' relative improvements. With 20 queries per model, these differences are well within sampling noise; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds is reported anywhere.

Comparison to prior work is limited to plain PGD. No transferability-enhancing baselines are evaluated (e.g., input transformations, momentum, model ensembling, EOT, or existing LLM-side transfer methods such as Guiding-not-Forcing, AmpleGCG), so the reader cannot judge whether FORCE's gains are competitive with simpler or existing techniques.

The causal chain 'layer/spectral reliance → sharp loss landscape → poor transfer' is argued correlationally. The weight-perturbation experiment (a 0.0002 shift) is only a rough proxy for transfer-induced parameter shifts, and no experiment directly ties early-layer or high-frequency reliance to measured target-model success.

The spectral rescaling rule (Eq. 7, w_m = min(1, ℓ_{m-1}/ℓ_m)) is a fairly ad hoc heuristic; the interaction between repeated FFT rescaling and PGD clipping is not analysed, and the computational overhead of masking M frequency bands and sampling N reference points per iteration is not quantified.

Several analysis figures are based on a single jailbreaking example rather than aggregated over many instances, raising concerns about representativeness; sample sizes for the loss-landscape and frequency-band studies are not stated.

Presentation issues remain: inconsistent capitalisation of model names in tables, typos ('11st', 'Togetherly', 'Jialbreaking' in Algorithm 1), duplicated Qwen-VL references, and the 'improvement' rows mixing relative and absolute magnitudes make tables harder to interpret.

The 'Query (↓)' metric is only loosely defined (average queries until success?), and its exact protocol in the multi-query setting is not fully specified, which hinders reproducibility of the reported efficiency gains.

strengths: The diagnostic analysis is the strongest part of the paper: the loss-landscape visualizations (Figure 2), the layer-wise feature interpolation experiments (Figure 3, Appendix Figure 7), and the frequency-band masking study across optimization iterations (Figure 4) form a coherent and reasonably novel empirical narrative linking high-sharpness regions, early-layer reliance, and high-frequency reliance to poor cross-model transferability.

The proposed method is well motivated by the analysis, and the two components (layer-aware regularization and spectral rescaling) are clearly specified, with ablations (Table 3) showing each component contributes non-trivially on the chosen setting.

The evaluation spans multiple architectures (adapter-based, early-fusion) and commercial models, and the paper considers two strictness levels (multi-query and zero-shot), plus a blank-initialization ablation, which is more thorough than many jailbreak papers.
The paper is generally readable, includes algorithms and hyperparameters (Appendix B), and contains an explicit ethics statement, which is appropriate for this type of red-teaming work.
weaknesses: The headline improvements are fragile. On early-fusion and commercial models the baseline ASRs are 1–5% and the '100–200% improvement' claims rest on 1→2 or 0→1 absolute changes with no statistical significance testing, no confidence intervals, and small evaluation sets (top 100/20 instructions). These differences are easily within run-to-run noise, so the central claim of improved transferability to the hardest targets is not convincingly supported.

Evaluation validity is undermined by the case studies. Figure 10 (GPT-5) shows a completely off-topic response about cannabis to an embezzlement question, yet it is presented as a successful jailbreak; Figure 9 (Gemini) is largely a defensive/educational response with a disclaimer. This casts serious doubt on the substring-matching + LLM-judge ASR pipeline and on whether reported ASRs measure genuinely harmful completions.

Missing baselines for the core problem. For a paper explicitly about improving attack transferability, the only baseline is plain PGD. Established transferability techniques (model ensembling, input transformations/EOT, momentum/variance-reduction methods, SAM-style sharpness minimization, or existing transferable jailbreak methods such as AmpleGCG-style approaches) are neither compared to nor discussed, so there is no evidence FORCE is better than simpler alternatives.

All analysis and attacks use a single source model (LLaVA-1.5-7B). The conclusions about early-layer and high-frequency reliance, and the method's design choices, could be source-specific; at minimum one additional source model would be needed to substantiate generality.

The method is largely heuristic: the layer weighting λl (Eq. 5), the reference-loss-weighted distance in Eq. 6 (the role of ℓref in the numerator is under-explained), and especially the ad hoc ratio wm = min(1, ℓm−1/ℓm) (Eq. 7) lack theoretical or ablation-based justification (e.g., sensitivity to N, η, λ, M). The weight-perturbation experiment (a 0.0002 perturbation 'simulating' transfer) is also a crude proxy for architecture changes that dominate real transfer.

The 'Query ↓' metric is never precisely defined (queries per successful attack? until success? capped at 100?), yet it accounts for half of the reported results; this ambiguity makes the efficiency claims unverifiable.

The improvements over the strongest absolute numbers are modest even on adapter-based targets (e.g., 61→64, 84→90), and the average '13% ASR improvement' framing mixes relative and absolute gains inconsistently across sections.
No code release is stated; combined with an unclarified judging pipeline and the questionable case studies, reproducibility of the results is uncertain.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly structured paper: the analysis-to-method pipeline (loss landscape sharpness -> layer feature interpolation -> frequency band analysis -> FORCE) is logically coherent and easy to follow.

The empirical analysis (Figures 2-4, 7) is informative: showing that visual jailbreaks sit in high-sharpness regions, that early-layer features have narrow feasible regions, and that high-frequency reliance grows during optimisation are interesting observations that go beyond simply proposing a new attack.

Broad evaluation coverage: two open-source architectures (adapter-based and early-fusion) plus three commercial models, three benchmarks, and multiple attack settings (multi-query, blank initialisation, zero-shot).

Ablation of the two components (Table 3) is present, and Figure 5/6 verify that the method actually produces the intended mechanistic effect (flatter layer feasible regions, reduced high-frequency reliance), not just better end metrics.
The paper is transparent about LLM usage, includes an ethics statement and reproducibility statement, and hyperparameters are specified.
weaknesses: Very narrow baseline comparison: the only baseline is plain PGD. The transferable-adversarial-example literature offers many standard baselines (MI-FGSM, input transformations such as DIM/TI, ensemble attacks, frequency-domain or attention-guided transfer attacks), none of which are compared. Without these, it is hard to judge whether the layered/spectral analysis is necessary to achieve the reported gains.

All experiments use a single source model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B). The claimed mechanism (model-specific feature reliance) and the generalisation of the findings cannot be verified against a different source architecture; conclusions may be source-model specific.

Absolute improvements on commercial models are very small (often 1-2% ASR, e.g., GPT-5: 1% -> 2%, Claude: 1% -> 2%), yet the text emphasises relative gains ('200% improvement', 'average improvement of 70%'). This framing overstates the practical significance; no statistical significance testing or variance over random seeds is reported anywhere.

Serious validity concern in the case studies: Figure 10 (GPT-5) shows the prompt asks about nonprofit embezzlement, but the model's response is about cannabis use - completely unrelated to the query. This suggests the attack broke instruction following rather than eliciting the requested harmful content, and it casts doubt on whether the ASR evaluation (substring matching + HarmBench classifier) correctly flags such off-topic responses as successes.

Computational cost is unreported. FORCE requires N=10 reference sample forward/backward passes plus M=10 frequency-masked forward passes per optimisation iteration (roughly 20x extra model evaluations per step vs. PGD); the 'query reduction' claims should be weighed against this per-iteration overhead, which is never quantified.

The layer regularisation objective (Eq. 6, Algorithm 2) mixes two goals in a ratio lambda_l * l_ref / d_l. The gradient incentives (jointly minimising reference loss and maximising feature distance) are plausible but not analysed; alternative formulations or sensitivity to lambda, N, and eta are not studied.

The causal claim that flat loss landscapes cause transferability is asserted from correlation (sharper for PGD, flatter for FORCE, better transfer for FORCE); no control experiment (e.g., another flatness-inducing regulariser) isolates whether flatness per se, rather than the specific feature corrections, drives the gains.

Only the zero-shot column of Table 2 shows the strictest setting, and improvements there are small for early-fusion and commercial models; the narrative that FORCE 'substantially' improves transferability is weakest precisely where it matters most (black-box frontier models).

Presentation issues: typos ('Jialbreaking' in Algorithm 1, '11st Layer', 'Togetherly', '11st'), and reference list contains duplicate entries (Bai et al. 2023a/b identical; Qwen-vl mislabelled). These are minor but suggest rushed preparation.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel problem framing: the paper is among the first to systematically study cross-model transferability of optimisation-based visual jailbreaking attacks, a practically relevant gap for red-teaming closed-source MLLMs.

The diagnostic analysis is a genuine contribution: the loss-landscape sharpness measurements (Fig. 2), layer-wise feature-interpolation experiments (Fig. 3, App. A/B), and frequency-band masking over optimisation iterations (Fig. 4, App. C) provide concrete, interpretable evidence for the claimed early-layer and high-frequency over-reliance, and are replicated on a second architecture in the appendix.

The proposed FORCE method follows directly from the analysis: layer-aware regularisation (Eqs. 3-6) and spectral rescaling (Eq. 7) are grounded in the two observed pathologies rather than being ad hoc, and Algorithm 1-3 make the method reproducible.

Broad empirical evaluation: 5 open-source targets spanning adapter-based and early-fusion architectures plus 3 commercial models (GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro), three benchmarks, zero-shot and multi-query settings, blank initialisation, comparisons with GCG, ensemble optimisation, MI-FGSM, DI-FGSM, and MLAI (Tables 1-2, 7-8), a component ablation (Table 3), cost analysis (Table 4), and robustness against noise-based defences (Table 9).

Consistent improvements in the setting where transfer actually works (adapter-based targets): ~12% average ASR gain and >15% query reduction over PGD, with an alternative source model confirming generality (Table 6), and positive component ablations showing each part contributes.
Clear writing with a logical progression from observation to method, and implementation released.
weaknesses: Absolute gains in the hardest and most safety-relevant settings are very small: on early-fusion models ASR moves from ~1-5% to ~2-11%, and on commercial models from ~1-10% to ~2-10% (Tables 1-2). The reported '70% average improvement' for commercial MLLMs is a relative statistic on near-floor baselines (e.g., 1.00→2.00 counts as 100%), so the claim of a 'firm step toward practical attacks' is overstated; the paper itself concedes in Appendix J that the method falls short against these models.

No statistical rigour: results appear to be single runs on small instruction subsets (top 100, top 20 for commercial models) with no confidence intervals, variance over seeds, or significance tests. Several 'improvements' are 1-2 ASR points, which could easily be noise.

The causal chain from sharpness/feature over-reliance to poor transferability is asserted more than demonstrated. The analysis is correlational; showing that FORCE flattens the landscape (Figs. 5-6) and improves transfer does not establish that flattening is the mechanism of transfer, and the weight-perturbation proxy for transfer is a loose model of cross-architecture shifts.

Several methodological choices are heuristic and under-justified: the quadratic layer-penalty schedule (Eq. 5), the β rule for frequency rescaling (Eq. 7), and the sensitivity of results to hyperparameters (e.g., λ must be retuned from 0.75 to 0.01 for a different source model in App. E) are not analysed, raising questions about robustness of the approach.

Some claimed efficiency numbers are questionable: spectral rescaling (Algorithm 3) requires M=10 additional forward passes per iteration, yet Table 4 reports only ~26% time overhead; and the regularisation term uses N=10 reference samples each needing a forward/backward pass — the 'negligible additional cost' claim deserves verification.

The main empirical story rests on a single source model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B); only one additional source is studied, and only on MaliciousInstruct. The 'universality' of the diagnosed pathologies is checked on only one further architecture (InstructBLIP).
Baselines in Table 8 are largely self-implemented rather than established transferable visual jailbreak methods (the authors note none exist), limiting external validation of the claimed superiority.

Ethical safeguards are thin for an attack paper: case studies display complete harmful outputs verbatim (Appendix I), and while limitations are discussed, there is no explicit responsible-disclosure or ethics statement addressing the dual-use risk of released code and prompts.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: improving cross-model transferability of optimisation-based visual jailbreaking attacks for red-teaming closed-source MLLMs, a topic of practical importance.

The diagnostic analysis (Section 3) is a genuine strength: the loss-landscape visualisation (Figure 2), layer-wise feature interpolation experiments (Figure 3), and frequency-band masking over the optimisation trajectory (Figure 4) provide a coherent, evidence-backed account of why PGD-style jailbreaks fail to transfer, and the analysis is replicated on a second architecture in Appendices B and C.

Broad empirical coverage: transfer to adapter-based, early-fusion, and commercial MLLMs (Table 1), multiple benchmarks, blank-initialisation and zero-shot settings (Table 2), component ablation (Table 3), computational cost (Table 4), and comparisons with ensemble/MI-FGSM/DI-FGSM/textual GCG baselines in Appendices E-H.
The limitations section (Appendix J) is candid, correctly noting that pixel-space perturbations map poorly to token-space vulnerabilities of early-fusion and commercial models.
The method is computationally cheap: reported overhead is modest (~26% time, ~12% memory) relative to baseline PGD.
weaknesses: Modest and statistically unsupported gains in the most important settings. On early-fusion and commercial models (the paper's stated motivation), absolute ASR improvements are 1-6 points (e.g., GPT-5: 1.00→2.00 on MaliciousInstruct, Claude: 1.00→2.00), and '100%'/'200%' improvements are differences of a single success on n=100 instructions, with no significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance across seeds reported. The claimed 'average improvement of 70%' for commercial models rests on such tiny baselines.

The zero-shot results (Table 2, right) largely undermine the flatness-transferability narrative in the strictest setting: FORCE improves over PGD by 0-6 points (26→26 on Llava-v1.6), even though a flatter loss landscape should help most precisely when a single attempt must align with target-model vulnerabilities. The paper's qualitative explanation is hand-wavy here.

Limited methodological novelty. The components are recombinations of established ideas: sharpness/flatness-motivated regularisation for transferability (cf. SAM-style arguments, ref. [47]), input-diversity-like neighbourhood sampling (cf. DI-FGSM [50]), and frequency-domain suppression of high-frequency components for transferable attacks (cf. [18]). The spectral rescaling rule in Eq. (7) is a heuristic without theoretical grounding, and the ablation (Table 3) shows the layer component alone contributes only 3.8% ASR.

Causal link between the analysis and the method is correlational. The weight-perturbation sharpness experiment (0.0002 perturbation on the source model) is a proxy for transfer-induced parameter shifts, but transfer across architectures involves far larger, structured parameter differences; the paper does not establish that sharpness is the mechanism rather than a correlate.

Hyperparameter sensitivity weakens the generality claim: the regularisation strength must be retuned per source model (λ=0.75 for LLaVA-v1.5 vs λ=0.01 for InstructBLIP, Appendix E), suggesting the layer-scale of the regulariser is fragile and that a practitioner cannot simply apply the method to a new source model.

Main-table results use only a single source model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B); the second-source experiment appears only in the appendix and shows near-zero transfer to early-fusion models for both methods (ASR 1-2%), reinforcing that the practical value for non-adapter targets is thin.

Presentation and rigour issues: Eq. (6) vs Algorithm 2 use inconsistent notation (fθ,l vs h, and ℓref vs ℓn), Algorithm 2 line 4 has malformed syntax, typos ('11st', 'Togetherly', 'Jialbreaking'), and the efficient-attack selection used for the multi-query setting (how attacks are selected/ordered for target models) is underspecified.

Dual-use and responsible-disclosure concerns are not addressed: the paper releases attack code, reports successful jailbreaks against GPT-5/Claude/Gemini, and prints verbatim harmful outputs (Appendix I) without discussing coordination with vendors, disclosure timing, or safeguards on released artefacts — a material omission for a paper whose stated goal is red-teaming.

strengths: The paper offers one of the first systematic analyses of why optimisation-based visual jailbreaking attacks fail to transfer across MLLMs. The three-pronged diagnosis — loss-landscape sharpness (Fig. 2), layer-wise feature interpolation (Fig. 3), and frequency-band masking over optimisation iterations (Fig. 4) — is coherent, novel within this problem area, and each observation is used to motivate a specific component of the method.

The proposed FORCE method is simple and directly grounded in the analysis: layer-aware regularisation on early-layer features and spectral rescaling of high-frequency components. Ablations (Table 3) show each component contributes individually and jointly, and Figures 5–6 verify that the method actually changes the intermediate properties it was designed to target, not just the end metric.

Evaluation breadth is above average: three open-source adapter-based targets, two early-fusion targets, and three commercial models (Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5), three benchmarks, two attack settings (multi-query, zero-shot), comparisons against textual GCG (Appendix F), strong visual baselines including ensemble/MI-PGD/DI-PGD/MLAI (Appendix G), robustness to noise defences (Appendix H), and a second source model (Appendix E). This is a fairly comprehensive empirical treatment.

The paper is transparent about negative results: it openly reports very low absolute ASR on early-fusion and commercial models and discusses this in the limitations section, and the 'improvement' framing is accompanied by raw ASR values so readers can see baseline levels.

Reproducibility appears good: full algorithms (Appendix D), explicit hyperparameters, dataset/evaluation protocol details (including LLM-based harmfulness judging with HarmBench classifier), and a stated code release.
weaknesses: The practical significance of the headline gains is limited. Average ASR improvements of ~12% on adapter-based models are meaningful, but on the hardest and most important targets (early-fusion and commercial MLLMs) absolute ASRs remain in the 1–11% range, and many 'improvement' percentages (e.g., 100%, 200%) are relative to baselines of 1–2%. The authors themselves concede in Appendix J that the method 'still falls short of a practical attack' on these models. The contribution is therefore more of an analysis-plus-incremental-improvement than a solution to the stated problem.

The causal story is asserted more than established. High-sharpness regions, early-layer narrow feasible regions, and high-frequency reliance are each shown, but the chain 'feature over-reliance → high sharpness → poor transferability' is correlational. In particular, weight-perturbation analysis on the source model (Fig. 2 bottom) is a crude proxy for the actual distribution shift across heterogeneous architectures, and the analysis cannot fully explain why the method still fails almost entirely on early-fusion models despite its generality claims.

Main experiments use a single source model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B). The second source model in Appendix E requires changing λ from 0.75 to 0.01 — a two-order-of-magnitude adjustment — suggesting the method has non-trivial hyperparameter sensitivity across architectures that is not ablated.

Statistical rigor is thin. Results appear to be single-run point estimates (e.g., ASR differences of 2–3 points on 100–520 instructions); no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing is reported, so some reported gains may be within noise. The qualitative reading of Figures 3–4 also appears to rely on a limited set of example instances.

Broader societal/ethical treatment is insufficient. The paper demonstrates successful jailbreaks of deployed commercial systems and includes harmful outputs as case studies (Appendix I), but there is no explicit ethics statement, no discussion of responsible disclosure to the affected vendors, and the improved attack itself is the primary deliverable — the defensive implications of the diagnostic findings (e.g., frequency-based filtering, layer-feature monitoring) are not explored.

Some methodological choices are under-justified: the ratio-of-losses form of the layer regularisation (Eq. 6), the β-scaling in Eq. 7, and the specific form of λ_l (Eq. 5) are presented without ablation or theoretical motivation; only the two component on/off ablations are given.

Presentation issues: the abstract claims attacks can be reliably improved against closed-source MLLMs, which overstates what Tables 1–2 show; reference list contains malformed entries (e.g., reference [2] with garbled page numbers); and terms like 'feasible region' are used loosely and inconsistently between input space and feature-space analyses.
